abstract: This paper studies residential electricity demand under Increasing Block Pricing (IBP) with intermittent billing, where cycle-level information on realized usage and billed charges becomes available only after a billing cycle ends. Using monthly billing records for 199,090 households served by the Sacramento Municipal Utility District between 2005 and 2008, I apply a sharp regression discontinuity (RD) design around the lower-tier Baseline Usage Quantity, where the marginal price rises discontinuously. The estimate indicates a reduction of 0.058 kWh/day in average daily consumption during the subsequent billing cycle, equivalent to about 0.26% of the local control-group mean. Under the RD assumptions, this estimate represents a local, cycle-averaged threshold-crossing effect near the cutoff. This ex post response coexists with the absence of sharp ex ante bunching in observed consumption, showing that the absence of sharp bunching need not imply the absence of price responsiveness under intermittent billing. The design does not distinguish among competing behavioral mechanisms, but the next-cycle timing pattern makes feedback timing a relevant consideration for nonlinear tariff design.
title: No bunching, yet response: Household electricity demand under increasing block pricing with intermittent billing

abstract: We study how firms choose to allocate control over strategic corporate decisions between shareholders and management in a historical setting where governance design was not mandated by corporate law, but ownership structures were constrained by differences in regional wealth distributions. The general shareholder meeting is the dominant governance body, retaining control over the largest number of strategic decisions. Nevertheless, firms with a predominance of small —and plausibly less informed— shareholders empower managers by delegating control over a larger number of strategic decisions to them. Furthermore, shareholder empowerment is accompanied by statutory provisions that facilitate information acquisition, suggesting that control and information are complements. Our findings highlight that the debate on shareholder empowerment should account for the role of ownership structure and information as key determinants of the allocation of control between shareholders and management.
title: Shareholder empowerment and ownership structure in a free-contracting environment

abstract: We introduce a probabilistic fine scheme into a simple model of a public bad with negative externalities. As the fine scheme is probabilistic, an agent’s probability to be fined depends on its relative action level. This creates an additional positive externality that could potentially restore efficiency by neutralising the negative externality from the public bad. In our analysis we derive conditions on the primitives of the model that guarantee the existence of an efficient equilibrium. We also demonstrate that a fine scheme can always be designed in such a way that an efficient outcome is induced in equilibrium.
title: Efficient probabilistic fines under negative externalities

abstract: We study a bilateral trade setting where a seller privately chooses quality, and a buyer may pay to verify it. We show that information acquisition by the buyer can give rise to an informational hold-up problem: when verification produces precise information, the seller shades quality, stripping the marginal buyer of surplus, causing trade to unravel. Trade survives only when verification is noisy enough to leave the buyer with residual surplus, yet precise enough to discipline the seller. The hold-up mechanism persists under buyer heterogeneity, noise in production, convex costs, and endogenous pricing.
title: Buyer Verification and Endogenous Quality

abstract: We investigate the impact of rising inequality on social instability through a novel multi-period laboratory experiment. In each period, members of two groups are randomly matched to play a battle of the sexes game, in which payoffs are either zero for both or positive but unequal. At the beginning of the game, the implied payoff inequality is low but, under some treatments, it increases over time. While under low initial inequality, unequal conventions – where one group is systematically better off – tend to emerge, increasing inequality causes destabilization. This is initiated by the group disadvantaged by the unequal convention and is particularly pronounced when not only the relative, but also the absolute position of the disadvantaged group is worsening. These findings are consistent with a simple model incorporating disadvantageous inequality aversion. Finally, we show that history matters; responses to current inequality depend on past experiences of inequality and stability.
title: Does increasing inequality threaten social stability? Evidence from the lab

abstract: Crowdsourcing-based decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) often aggregate members’ information and beliefs through token-weighted voting. Existing research shows that token-weighted voting erodes information aggregation when members vote myopically, whereas strategic members adjust the weight on their private signals inversely to their token holdings to unravel the weighting mechanism. We test voters’ behavior in a controlled experiment, finding that participants vote myopically, conservatively weighting their private signals, and that the voting mechanism does not influence their propensity to act strategically. Our results provide an important first step in developing a behavioral understanding of DAOs.
title: Behavioral Tokenomics: Myopic Voting and Token-Weighted Governance

abstract: We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.
title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures

abstract: We examine the long-term labor market consequences of exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War, focusing on cohorts whose childhoods overlapped the spraying period. Exploiting district-level variation in herbicide exposure intensity, we find exposed individuals attain lower levels of schooling and reduce their labor supply by 7% relative to the mean. Among individuals who remain in their birth provinces, labor income is reduced by 26.7%. We show that cognitive and physical health impairments do not fully explain the effects. Exposure also reduced household income and pushed individuals toward primary industries, away from wage employment. We further document intergenerational effects, as children of exposed parents exhibit lower educational attainment and reduced labor supply. These findings highlight the lasting and multigenerational economic costs of wartime chemical exposure.
title: The unseen pain of the Vietnam War: long-term effects of Agent Orange on labor market outcomes

abstract: This paper presents a finite-horizon, multiperiod, dynamic model of a durable goods market where owners have private information about product quality. We model product quality as changing stochastically over time and do not require monotonic depreciation. Purchase decisions depend on the endogenous quality distributions of the different types of goods for sale. The framework allows for multiple sources of nonstationarity such as changes in obsolescence and external supply over time. The market equilibrium is defined by prices, quantities, and the quality distributions of the different types of durable goods available for purchase. We use a fixed-point method to provide a formal proof of the existence of equilibrium. We discuss the challenges of computational applications and report a numerical implementation for a stylized 20-period discrete version of the model. Because we allow equilibrium to be nonstationary and quality to change non-monotonically, our framework can be extended to the housing market, the marriage market, and other markets where unobservable quality influences the product or relationship’s value over time.

abstract: The expansion of intermittent renewable electricity increases supply variability and requires greater flexibility from consumers. This results in welfare losses for agents who are averse to fluctuations. Our model analyzes these welfare consequences by considering short-term and exogenous variability in renewable energy generation. We explore an optimal control problem that determines a welfare-maximizing electricity consumption path by controlling dispatchable energy and storage. This optimization problem identifies three scenarios: no active storage, abundant storage capacities and limited capacities. We then derive an overall consumer welfare function for alternative energy mixes. This allows us to assess the welfare effects of changing the energy mix. In particular, we consider the substitution of dispatchable fossil-fueled energy generation by renewable energy.

abstract: The AI boom is usually discussed as a contest over models, chips, and productivity. This column argues that it is also a large physical infrastructure and credit cycle. The policy priority is not to call the peak, but to measure who owns the assets, who owes the debt, and where contingent obligations will land if demand disappoints.
abstract_zh: 人工智能热潮通常被讨论为一场围绕模型、芯片和生产率的竞赛。本专栏认为，它同时也是一场规模庞大的实体基础设施与信贷周期。政策优先事项不是判断峰值何时到来，而是衡量谁拥有这些资产、谁背负债务，以及如果需求令人失望，或有负债将落在何处。
title: Financing the AI buildout before the risks go off balance sheet

abstract: High public debt in several euro-area countries has renewed the debate over a central question: can fiscal pressures in one member state affect inflation expectations elsewhere by constraining the ECB? This column uses a randomised information experiment with German firms to show that the answer depends on trust in the central bank. Pessimistic debt projections for France, Italy, and Spain raise the three-year inflation expectations of firms that distrust the ECB, while high-trust firms do not react. By contrast, a €500 billion German debt package leaves inflation expectations unchanged.
abstract_zh: 几个欧元区国家的高公共债务重新引发了对一个核心问题的辩论：一个成员国的财政压力能否通过约束欧洲央行来影响其他地区的通胀预期？本专栏利用一项针对德国企业的随机信息实验表明，答案取决于对中央银行的信任。对法国、意大利和西班牙的悲观债务预测，会提高那些不信任欧洲央行的企业的三年期通胀预期，而高信任度的企业则没有反应。相比之下，一项5000亿欧元的德国债务计划并未使通胀预期发生变化。
authors: Francesco Bianchi, Renato Faccini, Leonardo Melosi, Nils Wehrhöfer
title: Your debt, my inflation: The role of trust in the ECB

abstract: This paper examines how invasion-related disruption reshapes the demand for digital skills. The analysis uses a novel dataset of millions of online job vacancies in Ukraine from 2021 to 2025 classified with large language models and mapped to the ESCO taxonomy. The paper links vacancy-level skill data to high-frequency ACLED attack intensity measures and estimate time-series models. The findings document a robust positive association between attack intensity and the digital skill share of job postings, consistent across specifications and alternative attack measures. Within- and between-occupation shifts and remote work adoption jointly drive this increase, with within-occupation reskilling and upskilling alone accounting for roughly half of the total rise. The growing digital skill share partly reflects the relative resilience of digital hiring against a broader contraction in the volume of vacancies. These findings carry concrete implications for digital reskilling policy, labor market monitoring, and recovery and reconstruction planning.
title: Labor Demand for Digital Skills in Post-2022 Ukraine: Evidence from Online Job Vacancy Data

abstract: This paper examines the impact of bank transparency on bank efficiency. Using the 2014 information disclosure rule for listed banks issued by the China Securities Regulatory Commission as an exogenous shock, we conduct a staggered difference-in-differences analysis using data on Chinese commercial banks from 2008 to 2023. We find that improved bank transparency reduces interest expenses and the cost-to-income ratios on the cost side, while increasing loan interest income, market power, and market share on the income side, thereby enhancing bank efficiency. This positive effect is more pronounced for less efficient banks and those with lower customer deposit ratios, as well as in regions with weaker financial regulation. Transparency also lowers bank risk and liquidity hoarding, with long-lasting efficiency gains. Overall, enhancing bank transparency supports stable and high-quality banking development, with valuable implications for global banking regulation and governance.
